sections.section_name: Section B - Very Short Analytical Concepts

questions.question_text: Explain why the atomic radius decreases as we move from left to right across a period in the periodic table. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Across a period, electrons are added to the same principal shell while the nuclear charge increases. This pulls the electron cloud closer, shrinking the atomic radius due to higher effective nuclear attraction.

questions.question_text: State the Law of Multiple Proportions and give one chemical example illustrating it. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: If two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other are in simple whole-number ratios. Example: Carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$) and Carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$).

questions.question_text: Define an intensive property in thermodynamics and provide two common examples. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: An intensive property is independent of the amount or size of the substance present in the system. Common examples include temperature, pressure, density, and refractive index.

questions.question_text: Based on VSEPR theory, predict the geometric shape and bond angle of the ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) molecule. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Ammonia possesses three bond pairs and one lone pair. Due to lone pair-bond pair repulsion, the basic tetrahedral geometry distorts into a trigonal pyramidal shape with a bond angle of roughly $107^\circ$.

questions.question_text: Calculate the molarity of a solution containing $4.0\text{ g}$ of sodium hydroxide ($\text{NaOH}$) dissolved in $250\text{ mL}$ of aqueous solution. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Molar mass of $\text{NaOH} = 40\text{ g/mol}$. Moles of $\text{NaOH} = \frac{4.0}{40} = 0.1\text{ mol}$. Volume in liters $= 0.25\text{ L}$. Molarity equals $\frac{0.1}{0.25} = 0.4\text{ M}$.

questions.question_text: A photon has a wavelength of $400\text{ nm}$. Calculate its energy in Joules. (Planck's constant $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$, speed of light $c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$). [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The energy of a photon is given by $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$. Substituting the values: $E = \frac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8)}{400 \times 10^{-9}} = 4.97 \times 10^{-19}\text{ Joules}$.

questions.question_text: Differentiate between an orbit and an orbital by listing three main contrasting points. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: 1. An orbit is a well-defined circular path, whereas an orbital is a 3D probability space. 2. Orbits violate Heisenberg's uncertainty principle; orbitals align with it. 3. Orbits lack directional characteristics, while orbitals (except s) possess specific spatial directions.

questions.question_text: Using Molecular Orbital Theory, explain why the $\text{He}_2$ molecule does not physically exist. Calculate its bond order. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Helium has an electronic configuration of $1s^2$. For $\text{He}_2$ (4 electrons), the MOT configuration is $\sigma_{1s}^2 \sigma^*_{1s}^2$. Bond order $= \frac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a) = \frac{1}{2}(2 - 2) = 0$. Since bond order is zero, the molecule is completely unstable.

questions.question_text: An organic compound contains $40\%$ carbon, $6.6\%$ hydrogen, and the rest is oxygen. Determine its empirical formula. (Atomic masses: $\text{C}=12$, $\text{H}=1$, $\text{O}=16$). [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Oxygen percentage $= 100 - (40 + 6.6) = 53.4\%$. Moles: $\text{C} = \frac{40}{12} = 3.33$; $\text{H} = \frac{6.6}{1} = 6.6$; $\text{O} = \frac{53.4}{16} = 3.33$. Dividing by the smallest (3.33), the simple ratio is $\text{C:H:O} = 1:2:1$. Empirical formula is $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$.

questions.question_text: Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of liquid water using the following data: $\Delta_c H^\circ(\text{C, graphite}) = -393.5\text{ kJ/mol}$, $\Delta_c H^\circ(\text{H}_2\text{, g}) = -285.8\text{ kJ/mol}$. State the required balanced chemical equation. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The formation equation for water is $\text{H}_2\text{(g)} + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$. The enthalpy of formation is identical to the enthalpy of combustion of hydrogen gas. Therefore, $\Delta_f H^\circ (\text{H}_2\text{O, l}) = -285.8\text{ kJ/mol}$ directly.

questions.question_text: Describe the hybridization process occurring in a methane ($\text{CH}_4$) molecule. What type of hybrid orbitals are formed? [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Carbon's ground state ($2s^2 2p^2$) promotes an electron to the empty $2p$ orbital, creating an excited state ($2s^1 2p^3$). These four orbitals mix completely to yield four equivalent $sp^3$ hybrid orbitals directed tetrahedrally, overlapping with hydrogen's $1s$ orbitals.

questions.question_text: State the Pauli Exclusion Principle and use it to determine the maximum capacity of a single atomic orbital. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The Pauli Exclusion Principle states that no two electrons in an atom can share the exact same set of four quantum numbers. Consequently, a single orbital can hold a maximum of only two electrons, and they must have opposite spins.

questions.question_text: Read the following case context: A researcher heats $50\text{ g}$ of calcium carbonate ($\text{CaCO}_3$) inside a sealed thermodynamic vessel. The solid decomposes completely into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas. Assuming standard conditions, calculate the mass of calcium oxide formed and the volume of carbon dioxide gas evolved at STP. (Molar mass of $\text{CaCO}_3 = 100\text{ g/mol}$). [40-50 words]
questions.answer: The balanced decomposition reaction is $\text{CaCO}_3\text{(s)} \rightarrow \text{CaO(s)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$. $50\text{ g}$ of $\text{CaCO}_3$ is $0.5\text{ mol}$. This produces exactly $0.5\text{ mol}$ of $\text{CaO}$, which equates to $0.5 \times 56 = 28\text{ g}$. It also produces $0.5\text{ mol}$ of $\text{CO}_2$ gas, occupying a volume of $0.5 \times 22.4 = 11.2\text{ Liters}$ at STP.

questions.question_text: Read the following case context: In an industrial setting, two distinct gases, $A$ and $B$, behave as ideal gases under low-pressure scenarios. An engineer notes that the root-mean-square (RMS) velocity of gas $A$ is four times the RMS velocity of gas $B$ at the exact same temperature. Derive the structural relationship between the molar masses of these two gases. [40-50 words]
questions.answer: The RMS velocity formula is $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$. Given $v_A = 4 v_B$, substituting the formula yields $\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M_A}} = 4 \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M_B}}$. Squaring both sides and canceling the constant terms yields $\frac{1}{M_A} = \frac{16}{M_B}$. Therefore, the molar mass relationship is $M_B = 16 M_A$.

sections.section_name: Section E - Long-Form Structural & Organic Synthesis

questions.question_text: Discuss the physical significance of the four quantum numbers ($n$, $l$, $m_l$, $m_s$). Write down the complete set of quantum numbers for the outermost valence electron in a potassium atom ($Z=19$). [50-60 words]
questions.answer: Principal ($n$) defines orbital size and main energy level. Azimuthal ($l$) defines the subshell 3D shape ($s, p, d, f$). Magnetic ($m_l$) determines the spatial orientation of the orbital. Spin ($m_s$) indicates the electron's spin direction. For Potassium ($Z=19$, $[Ar] 4s^1$), the outermost electron is in $4s$. Thus, $n = 4$, $l = 0$, $m_l = 0$, $m_s = +1/2$ (or $-1/2$).

questions.question_text: Derive the mathematical relationship between the heat capacity at constant pressure ($C_p$) and heat capacity at constant volume ($C_v$) for an ideal gas. Show all necessary thermodynamic steps. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: Enthalpy is defined as $H = U + PV$. For one mole of an ideal gas, $PV = RT$, yielding $H = U + RT$. Differentiating with respect to temperature $T$, we get $\frac{dH}{dT} = \frac{dU}{dT} + R$. By thermodynamic definition, $\frac{dH}{dT} = C_p$ and $\frac{dU}{dT} = C_v$. Substituting these yields the fundamental relation $C_p = C_v + R$, or $C_p - C_v = R$.

questions.question_text: Explain the concept of Resonance using the carbonate ion ($\text{CO}_3^{2-}$) as a chemical example. Draw its contributing resonance structures and describe the actual nature of the carbon-oxygen bonds. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: Resonance occurs when a single Lewis structure cannot adequately represent a molecule's true properties. For $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, three equivalent structures exist, moving the double bond between the central carbon and different oxygen atoms. The true structure is a resonance hybrid, an average of these forms. Consequently, all three C-O bonds are completely identical, possessing a partial double-bond character with a bond order of $1.33$.
